Title: Discriminative power of organ-specific SOFA assessment in burn sepsis: A temporal biomarker analysis.

Journal/Date: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries (2026)

--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Severe burn patients face diagnostic challenges in distinguishing sepsis from systemic inflammation using Sepsis-3 criteria. Current Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) validation studies focus on composite scores, neglecting subsystem-level analysis in burn-specific pathophysiology.
[METHODS]: This retrospective cohort study analyzed 55 severe burn patients (TBSA>30 %) from a Chinese burn center (2021-2022), comparing 19 sepsis cases with 36 controls. We analyzed SOFA subsystems and biomarkers (creatinine, platelet count, NT-proBNP, and PCT) during both the early phase (days 1 and 3 post-burn) and the late phase (after day 3 post-burn), performed TBSA-adjusted logistic regression, and constructed a nomogram.
[RESULTS]: Cardiovascular (84.2 % vs 2.8 %, p < 0.001), renal (31.6 % vs 0 %, p < 0.001), and coagulation (42.1 % vs 5.6 %, p < 0.001) subsystems showed superior diagnostic specificity. Platelet trajectories revealed critical divergence at day 3 (septic: 66 vs control: 120 ×10⁹/L, p < 0.001), while creatinine elevation persisted across phases (day 1: 100 vs 62 μmol/L, p < 0.001, day 3: 84 vs 65 μmol/L, and late phase: 118 vs 58μmol/L, p < 0.001). PCT demonstrated isolated diagnostic utility confined to the late phase (6.12 vs 0.55 μg/L, p < 0.001). Day 3 platelet count, late-phase creatinine, and PCT were incorporated into the nomogram, which achieved an AUC of 0.930 in ROC analysis.
[CONCLUSION]: Subsystem-specific SOFA analysis identifies creatinine elevation and thrombocytopenia as key sepsis indicators in burns. Serial platelet and creatinine monitoring from day 3 post-injury enhances early detection, while PCT demonstrates diagnostic utility only in the late phase. --- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Platelet cells, or thrombocytes, have additional roles to haemostasis. After burn injury, platelet counts drop to a nadir at days 2-5 then rise to a peak between days 10-18. The nadir has previously been associated with mortality but there is currently no thorough investigation of its potential to predict sepsis in adults. The primary objective of this study is to assess whether platelet count can predict survival and sepsis in adults with severe burn injuries.
[METHODS AND FINDINGS]: A retrospective cohort analysis of platelet count and other blood parameters in 145 burn patients with a TBSA greater than 20%. AUROC analysis revealed that the platelet count and rBaux score together produce moderate discrimination for survival at less than 24h after injury (AUROC=0.848, 95%CI 0.765-0.930). Platelet count at day 3 combined with TBSA has a modest association with sepsis (AUROC=0.779, 95%CI 0.697-0.862). Multivariable Cox regression analysis revealed platelet peak was the strongest predictor of mortality.
[CONCLUSIONS]: A reduced peak platelet count is a strong predictor of 50-day mortality. Platelet count nadir may have some association with sepsis.

key_findings.finding: Adult severe-burn cohort (PMID 29032970; n=145, TBSA >20%) found that platelet count on post-burn day 3 combined with TBSA had modest discrimination for sepsis (AUROC 0.779, 95% CI 0.697–0.862). The abstract describes the normal trajectory as a nadir on days 2–5 followed by a peak on days 10–18, but does not establish a duration/persistence threshold or report thrombocytopenia as an independently adjusted predictor of sepsis; multivariable Cox analysis instead identified reduced platelet peak as the strongest predictor of 50-day mortality.

key_findings.finding: A newer retrospective Chinese cohort (PMID 41297233; n=55, TBSA >30%; 19 sepsis, 36 controls) showed marked day-3 platelet separation (66 vs 120 ×10^9/L, p<0.001). Coagulation SOFA abnormalities were more common in sepsis (42.1% vs 5.6%), and a model including day-3 platelets, late creatinine, and late procalcitonin achieved AUC 0.930; however, the abstract does not provide the platelet-specific adjusted odds ratio, threshold, sensitivity, or specificity, so independence of thrombocytopenia cannot be determined.

source_tools.relevance: Direct temporal burn-sepsis cohort with TBSA-adjusted logistic modeling and model performance

key_findings.finding: The pediatric severe-burn case-control study (PMID 8418782; 32 nonsurvivors versus 32 survivors with lethal burns) reported that platelet decline preceded other sepsis signs in all cases; <0.1 ×10^12/L occurred in 31/32 nonsurvivors versus 10/32 survivors, and persistence below that level for >4 days was uniformly associated with death. The authors called platelet count an independent predictor of sepsis and death, but the abstract does not provide adjusted effect estimates, a formal sepsis case definition, or diagnostic accuracy statistics; all deaths were interpreted as multisystem-organ-failure/sepsis, limiting causal and diagnostic specificity.

source_tools.relevance: Direct duration/threshold evidence in severe-burn patients

key_findings.finding: A 2024 retrospective severe-burn study (PMID 38535003; n=90; mean TBSA 48.7%; 60-day mortality 64.4%) found thrombocytopenia and platelet counts were worse in nonsurvivors at essentially all time points; sepsis occurred in about one-third, and in septic nonsurvivors thrombocytopenia did not normalize before death. This supports persistent thrombocytopenia as a marker of adverse trajectory and sepsis-associated mortality, but the reported evidence is associative: no sepsis-specific threshold, duration effect estimate, diagnostic AUROC, or multivariable demonstration that thrombocytopenia independently predicts sepsis was available.

source_tools.relevance: Daily platelet measurements and persistence/non-normalization in severe burns with sepsis subgroup
Primary abstract and cohort characteristics

key_findings.finding: Overall, continuous/persistent thrombocytopenia appears clinically meaningful mainly as an early warning and severity/prognostic marker, with the strongest burn-specific signal around post-burn day 3 and persistence during the subsequent course. Evidence that it independently predicts incident sepsis after adjustment is insufficient and inconsistent: the adult study provides only modest combined discrimination, the newer study reports a multivariable nomogram without platelet-specific coefficients, and the pediatric claim of independence lacks adjusted statistics. Major limitations are retrospective single-center designs, small cohorts, heterogeneous age/severity, confounding by TBSA and critical illness/coagulopathy, incomplete sepsis definitions, and limited reporting of thresholds, calibration, sensitivity/specificity, and external validation.
